prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification of topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect.

statement.case_for: After the full round-1 exchange I keep B041 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and my configuration is unchanged. Six of eight members now prefer B041 and all six credit Kane and Molenkamp, but I rest the case on the science. The Kane-Mele Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal introduced spin-orbit-driven band topology as an organising principle. Molenkamp's HgTe/CdTe transport measurement of quantised edge conductance turned that into a laboratory fact, so the chain from prediction to first observation is one coherent discovery. Fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and scanning probes, and the spread of the concept into hybrid superconducting structures, photonics and materials searches, make this mature. The citation can be written around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification, which is the part the three names actually carry, and can say openly that it does not adjudicate the three-dimensional or quantum anomalous Hall stories.
statement.case_against: The credit is still imperfect and I do not think round 1 resolved it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp measured, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy are central to the 3D theory; none can be named within three people. Hasan's ARPES result is a strong independent claim that my trio omits. Whether the 2016 topological phase transition prize already covers enough of the conceptual background to weaken the case is a real question: I read that prize as covering topological phases in one-dimensional chains and the quantum Hall plateaus, not the time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators or their material realisations, but I do not claim certainty. B013 is a cleaner two-name attribution and a sharper invention, and if the committee valued precision and testability over conceptual breadth I would regard it as a fully defensible prize.

responses.point: Danielsson credits Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan and holds that the experimental side of the field deserves two slots, so that the three-dimensional ARPES discovery is part of the core.
responses.response: I have thought about the chair's question on this and I still prefer Mele over Hasan, for a reason that goes beyond tidiness. The quantum spin Hall proposal in graphene and the Z2 invariant are a joint Kane-Mele result, and the 3D classification by Fu, Kane and Mele is built on it. Hasan's ARPES work is an excellent confirmation of a prediction that Fu, Kane and Mele and Moore and Balents had already made, so crediting it under the three-name limit leaves out theorists whose claim is at least as strong. I accept your point that the 3D materials are what made the field a materials-science programme, and I would be willing to have the citation say 'topological insulators' in its framing sentence only if that does not imply that Hasan is credited. If the committee instead prefers to extend the experimental side, I would want that discussed openly as a choice to drop Mele, not presented as a neutral substitution.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B013 (Katori and Ye) and frames the decision as whether conceptual reorganisation outweighs a compact invention with concrete testable consequences, while saying he would not oppose B041.
responses.response: This is the criterion the chair asked about, and I think it can be answered without dismissing your case. The Nobel Prize asks for a discovery or invention of the greatest benefit, and both qualify. I weigh B041 higher because the Z2 classification changed what condensed-matter physicists look for, whereas a lattice clock improves a measurement that already existed, even though the improvement is spectacular and the tests of relativity and constants are real. I am not persuaded by the sequencing worry that choosing B041 now crowds B013 out: the field is large enough for both in successive years. I also note that your possible Hall-group conflict does not touch my reasoning, and if the committee decides B013 is the finalist I would treat it as a strong prize. Where I cannot yet agree is that the redefinition of the second, which has not happened, should carry weight; I would leave it out of any citation.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength idea and the many-atom stability gain are new relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, so a lattice clock citation should be written narrowly around the lattice scheme.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that a narrow citation on the magic-wavelength lattice and its accuracy is the right wording; I do not regard adjacency to those prizes as disqualifying. My concern is the third helping of precision metrology that Kroll himself raises, and the fact that Ye's other work (B007) appears on a separate ballot, which suggests the Katori and Ye split will need a clear justification of why Ye's contribution is the lattice clock and not the broader programme. That is a presentation problem for B013, not a scientific objection, and it is why I list B013 first among my alternatives. For B041 I accept your point that the committee should word the attribution carefully, and I would apply the same discipline there by naming the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification explicitly.

responses.point: Olsson calls the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission the fairest statement of the attribution problem and says it cannot be fully resolved within the credited names.
responses.response: I agree and I think we should say so in the committee's record instead of hiding it. The HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what led Molenkamp's group to the quantum wells, and Zhang's death means that a prize naming him is no longer possible in any case, which matters for the posthumous-credit rule rather than for the science. The remaining question is whether two surviving co-authors, Bernevig and Hughes, would be fairly left out: in my view the Kane-Mele proposal came first and is conceptually broader, and BHZ is a specific materials prediction that Molenkamp's team tested, but I admit that this is a contestable judgment. Your point that the citation should cover the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators broadly matches how I have worded mine.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B029 to B041 after the opening ballots and describes B041 as a tighter story than a prize that also includes the quantum anomalous Hall effect.
responses.response: I welcome the move and agree that B029 and B041 should be treated as one achievement for voting purposes. Xue's quantum anomalous Hall observation is a real result but a derived realisation that needs magnetic doping and very low temperatures, and including it would force Mele out. I would not put Xue in any citation, and I do not think the committee should treat the QAH effect as a reason to reopen B029 as a separate part, since a two-part configuration would also exceed the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts Mele or Hasan in the third slot; I am confident of my choice but it remains a judgment call on which reasonable members differ.
How far the 2016 prize covers the conceptual ground of B041; I rely on my recollection of its scope, not on a verified source.
My recollection of the 2D and 3D chronology and of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Kane-Mele timeline is unverified.
Whether the uncredited originators of the HgTe and 3D theory can be handled adequately by citation wording alone.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B041, B013 or B026 from the provided profile. For B046 (circuit QED) I have field and institutional proximity: I work in circuit and waveguide QED, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and Chalmers hosted researchers linked to the 2025 prize, so I would consider recusal or at least caution if B046 were taken up. B046 is not in my configuration or alternatives.
